sub: Named after “the night” (al-layl), its first word
theme: People’s efforts are as different as night and day. The giver who fears Allah is eased toward good and saved; the stingy denier is eased toward hardship and the Fire.
story: Revealed in Makkah, around the same time as Ash-Shams, which it closely resembles.
Most reports say its closing ayat are about Abū Bakr. He bought persecuted Muslim slaves, such as Bilāl, whom Umayyah ibn Khalaf tortured under a rock, and set them free for Allah’s sake alone.
Another report ties the surah to Abū ad-Daḥdāḥ, who gave a whole garden for a disputed palm tree so its neighbours would have it, hoping for a palm in Paradise, after its owner had refused.

sections.title: Your efforts are worlds apart
sections.meaning: Allah swears by the night that covers, the day that shines, and the creation of male and female. These are pairs of opposites, and so are people’s efforts: some work toward Paradise, others toward the Fire.
points: By the night that covers and the day that shines
By the One who created male and female
sections.matters: It sets up the whole surah. Everyone is busy striving, but toward very different ends. The rest of the surah shows the two kinds of effort and where each one leads.
sections.story: Reportedly the two efforts were those of Abū Bakr, who bought and freed Bilāl, and Umayyah ibn Khalaf, who tortured him. Another report names Abū ad-Daḥdāḥ and a man who refused to give up a palm tree.
explained: The night covers everything in darkness and people rest. The day shines and they go out to work. Allah made male and female in pairs so each kind carries on. These opposites lead to the answer: your efforts are shattā, scattered and far apart.
Every morning, everyone sets out. By what they do, some are freeing themselves and some are destroying themselves. Opposite efforts cannot end in the same place.
teaches: Everyone is busy; ask where your effort is heading.
Good and evil deeds lead to opposite ends.
Each day you either free yourself or ruin yourself.
sections.hook: The oaths come in pairs: layl/nahār, dhakar/unthā. They set up shattā, “scattered”, in ayah 4, which the next section splits into two matching halves.

sections.title: Two roads, each made easy
sections.meaning: Whoever gives, fears Allah and believes in the best, Allah eases toward ease. Whoever is stingy, thinks he needs no one and denies the best, Allah eases toward hardship. And when he falls, his wealth will not help him.
points: Gives, fears Allah, believes the best → eased toward ease
Withholds, feels self-sufficient, denies → eased toward hardship
His wealth won’t help him when he falls
sections.matters: Three qualities against three. Deeds shape the road: the more you give and believe, the easier good becomes; the more you hold back, the easier evil becomes.
sections.story: Reportedly about Abū Bakr, who freed weak Muslim slaves only for Allah’s sake. One report says ayah 8 describes Umayyah ibn Khalaf.
explained: The first person aʿṭā wa ittaqā: gives what Allah asks, from zakah to charity, and guards against sin. He believes in al-ḥusnā, the best: lā ilāha illā Allāh and its reward. Allah eases him toward al-yusrā, so good comes easily, ending in Paradise.

The second is stingy, feels no need of Allah, and denies the best. He is eased toward al-ʿusrā: evil comes easily and good feels heavy. Asked why act if all is written, the Prophet ﷺ said, “Act, for each is eased toward what he was created for,” and recited these ayat.
teaches: Stinginess and feeling self-sufficient harden the heart.
Keep acting: each is eased toward what he was made for.
Wealth stays behind; only deeds go with you.
sections.hook: Two mirror sets of three: aʿṭā/bakhila, ittaqā/istaghnā, ṣaddaqa/kadhdhaba. Then the same fa-sanuyassiruhu with one letter changed: yusrā (7) becomes ʿusrā (10).

sections.title: The blazing Fire and who is spared
sections.meaning: Allah takes it on Himself to make guidance clear, and both lives belong to Him. So He warns of a blazing Fire that only the most wretched enters: the one who denied and turned away. The most pious is kept far from it: he gives to purify himself, for Allah alone, and he will be pleased.
points: Guidance is on Us; both lives belong to Us
A blazing Fire for the one who denied and turned away
The most pious, who gives to purify himself, is spared
Repaying no favour, only for Allah; he will be pleased
sections.matters: It closes with the two ends, matching section 2: the stingy denier ends in the Fire, and the sincere giver is spared. The final promise, “he will be pleased,” rewards giving for Allah alone.
sections.story: Most reports say ayat 17–21 were revealed about Abū Bakr. He bought persecuted Muslim slaves, including Bilāl, and freed them. When the idolaters claimed he was repaying Bilāl a favour, ayah 19 answered them.
explained: Showing guidance is Allah’s job, and this life and the next are His, so seek both from Him alone. He warns of a Fire that blazes. Only al-ashqā burns in it forever: the one who denied the truth and turned away from acting on it.

Al-atqā is kept far from it. He gives his wealth to purify himself, not to repay anyone or to be seen. He seeks only the Face of his Lord Most High. And he will surely be pleased with what Allah gives him.
teaches: Seek this world and the next from Allah alone.
Give to purify yourself, not to be praised.
Sincere giving expects nothing back from people.
Denying in the heart and turning away in action lead to the Fire.
sections.hook: Al-ashqā (15) and al-atqā (17) are matching opposites. The last ayah, wa la-sawfa yarḍā, is echoed at the start of the next surah: fa-tarḍā (93:5).

groups.text: By the night when it covers, and the day when it shines.
By the One who created male and female: your efforts are far apart.
Whoever gives, fears Allah and believes in the best, Allah eases toward ease.
Whoever is stingy, feels no need and denies the best, Allah eases toward hardship.
His wealth will not help him when he falls.
Making guidance clear is on Allah, and this life and the next are His.
A blazing Fire awaits the most wretched, who denied and turned away.
The most pious is kept from it: he gives to purify himself, repaying no one.
He gives only seeking his Lord’s Face, and he will be pleased.

1.explain: By the night when yaghshā: it covers creation with its darkness, and everyone goes home to rest from their work.

2.explain: By the day when tajallā: it shines out, and people spread out to their work in its light.

3.explain: Wa mā khalaqa: by the One who created male and female, or by His creating them: Adam and Ḥawwāʾ, and every male and female, paired so each kind carries on.

4.explain: The point of the oaths: saʿyakum la-shattā, your efforts are far apart. As night and day, male and female differ, some work for Paradise and some for the Fire.
4.why: Reportedly the differing efforts were those of Abū Bakr, who bought and freed Bilāl, and Umayyah ibn Khalaf. Another report names Abū ad-Daḥdāḥ, who bought a palm tree with his garden, and the owner who had refused to give it up.

5.explain: Aʿṭā: gives what he is told to give, from zakah to charity. Ittaqā: fears Allah and avoids what He forbade.
5.why: Reportedly about Abū Bakr, who freed weak Muslim slaves in Makkah. His father urged him to free strong men who could protect him; he answered that he wanted only what is with Allah.

6.explain: Ṣaddaqa bil-ḥusnā: he believes in the best. Either lā ilāha illā Allāh, or Paradise, or the reward Allah promised, or that Allah will replace what he spends.

7.explain: Fa-sanuyassiruhu lil-yusrā: We will ease him toward ease. Good deeds become easy and evil becomes hard, and the road ends in Paradise.

8.explain: Bakhila: withholds what he should give. Istaghnā: thinks he has no need of his Lord or His reward.
8.why: One report says it refers to Umayyah ibn Khalaf. In the palm-tree report, it is the man who refused to give his palm for one in Paradise.

9.explain: Kadhdhaba bil-ḥusnā: he denies the best, the reward of the Hereafter and the truth of lā ilāha illā Allāh.

10.explain: Lil-ʿusrā: toward hardship. Evil becomes easy for him and good feels heavy, and the road ends in the Fire.

11.explain: Taraddā: when he falls, into the grave at death or into the Fire. The wealth he hoarded won’t help him; only good deeds go with him.

12.explain: Inna ʿalaynā lal-hudā: it is on Us to make guidance clear, to show what is lawful and forbidden. Or: whoever takes the path of guidance reaches Allah.

13.explain: The Hereafter and this first life both belong to Allah. So seek both from Him; whoever seeks them from anyone else has lost the way.

14.explain: So I warn you, people of Makkah, of a Fire that talaẓẓā: blazes and flares.

15.explain: None will yaṣlāhā, enter and burn in it forever, except al-ashqā, the most wretched. Sinful believers may be punished for a time, but staying forever is for the disbeliever.

16.explain: …who kadhdhaba, denied the truth with his heart, and tawallā, turned away from faith and from acting on it.

17.explain: Al-atqā, the most God-fearing, will be kept far from the Fire.
17.why: Most reports say ayat 17–21 are about Abū Bakr, who spent heavily buying persecuted Muslim slaves, seven of them, and freeing them. The wording is general and covers anyone who gives like him.

18.explain: …who gives his wealth yatazakkā: to purify himself, for Allah alone, not to be seen or praised.

19.explain: No one has done him a favour that he is paying back. His giving is not a return for anything done for him.
19.why: When Abū Bakr bought and freed Bilāl, whom Umayyah ibn Khalaf tortured under a great rock, the idolaters claimed he did it to repay a favour Bilāl had done him. This ayah answered them.

20.explain: Illā ibtighāʾa wajhi rabbihi al-aʿlā: only seeking the Face of his Lord, the Most High, hoping to see Him in Paradise.

21.explain: Wa la-sawfa yarḍā: and he will surely be pleased with the reward Allah gives him in Paradise.
